description: On daemon start, a bundled action the user has not edited is brought up to the repo version, and a bundled action missing from ~/.outpost/actions/ is installed, so the daemon never runs a stale copy.
steps: Merge a change to an existing bundled action's SKILL.md (e.g. meta.orchestrate) and add a new bundled action dir, without touching ~/.outpost/actions/ by hand
Pull main in ~/github/frostbyte73/outpost and run launchctl kickstart -k gui/$UID/local.outpost.$USER
Open the Actions page: the edited action shows the merged text and the new action is listed
diff -r the two actions' repo dirs against ~/.outpost/actions/: no differences

description: A bundled action whose installed copy the user has edited is left alone on daemon start and reported in the daemon log and on the Actions page.
steps: Edit ~/.outpost/actions/<category>/<name>/SKILL.md for one bundled action
Merge a different change to the same action in the repo, pull main and restart the daemon
The installed SKILL.md still holds the user's edit, byte for byte
The daemon log names the action as user-edited and not updated
The Actions page marks the same action as user-edited / not synced

description: A job asking for a whole project (new or existing repo) is planned in meta.orchestrate's project category: shaping steps (project.shape, project.requirements, project.decompose), then milestones as meta.job children whose briefs name docs/projects/<slug>/ and the files to read.
steps: Create a job: 'Make a small browser game: <one-paragraph idea>'
Open the plan at plan_pending_review: its findings name the project category
The plan has project.shape, project.requirements and project.decompose steps before any code step
After decompose, each milestone is a meta.job step whose brief names docs/projects/<slug>/ and lists the files the child must read
Every code step in the plan traces to at least one feature ID

description: A one-ticket job keeps its short path: no project category, no shaping steps, no project folder.
steps: Create a job for a one-line bug fix in this repo
Open the plan at plan_pending_review
It has no project.* or meta.job steps and creates no docs/projects/ folder; the work is a single code.orchestrate-pr step

description: project.shape turns an idea into a one-page brief.md (problem, audience, appetite, no-gos, rabbit holes, success criteria), writing [NEEDS CLARIFICATION] instead of guessing and returning those questions as clarifications[]; when there are any, the plan follows it with a meta.wait and a second project.shape.
steps: Create a project job from a deliberately vague idea (no audience, no time budget)
Open the project.shape output: brief.md has all six sections and fits on one page
The missing facts appear as [NEEDS CLARIFICATION: ...] markers in brief.md and as entries in clarifications[]
The plan has a meta.wait after shape and a second project.shape after it

description: project.requirements writes features.json from brief.md: one entry per user-visible behaviour with end-to-end steps and passes:false; a re-run keeps existing IDs and passes values, numbers new entries above the highest ID, and marks removed features dropped instead of deleting them.
steps: Run a project job through project.requirements and open its output
Every entry has id, category, description, steps and passes:false; the steps describe what a person does and sees
No entry covers something the brief lists as a no-go
Edit the brief to remove one behaviour and add another, then re-run project.requirements
The removed feature is still present with dropped:true; the new one takes the next F-NNN; every other entry's id and passes are unchanged

description: project.decompose writes roadmap.md as a milestone dependency graph (thinnest end-to-end slice first, riskiest unknown next), each milestone with a standalone meta.job brief and the feature IDs it must pass, and its milestones[] map straight onto meta.job steps.
steps: Run a project job through project.decompose and open roadmap.md in its output
Milestone 1 is an end-to-end slice a person can run, not a layer such as 'set up the database'
Milestone 2 addresses the brief's riskiest rabbit hole
Each milestone lists its dependencies, a brief readable without the rest of the roadmap, and its feature IDs
Every non-dropped feature ID appears in at least one milestone
The plan's following meta.job steps match milestones[] one for one

description: write.create-repo creates frostbyte73/<name> private by default (public only when the job says so) through an approved write draft, then clones and registers it like write.add-project.
steps: Create a job that needs a new repo, without mentioning visibility
At the write draft, the exact create command names frostbyte73/<name> and private visibility
Approve it: github.com/frostbyte73/<name> exists, is private, and has a README on its default branch
The repo is cloned outside ~/.outpost/worktrees and appears in Outpost's project list
Repeat with a job that says 'public': the draft asks for public visibility

description: The repo-create grant is pinned to the frostbyte73 owner: a create under any other owner is refused even after the user approves a draft.
steps: Create a job that asks write.create-repo for someorg/<name>
The action refuses or the permission gate denies the call; no repo is created under someorg

description: The files the project.* actions return land in docs/projects/<slug>/ through a code.orchestrate-pr PR byte for byte, the latest step's copy winning when two steps emit the same path.
steps: Run a project job through shape, requirements and decompose, and on to the PR that commits the folder
For each path, compare the PR's file with the newest previousSteps files[] entry for it: identical bytes
Where shape ran twice, the PR holds the second shape's brief.md

description: Marking a meta.session Done from the job's step card (work/step-card.js) offers a note field, and the typed note is sent with Done, on desktop and mobile.
steps: Run a job to a meta.session step
Open the job; the session step's card shows a note field beside Done
Type 'Audience is me; budget two weekends' and click Done
The step resolves with output {resumed_by: "user", note} carrying that text
Repeat on mobile: the pushed job screen shows the same field and Done sends the note

description: Marking a meta.session Done from the desktop cockpit board (cockpit/bodies.js) offers a note field, and the typed note is sent with Done. Desktop only: mobile mounts the inbox, whose rows open the job, where the step card's field (F-011) carries the note.
steps: Run a job to a meta.session step
Open the cockpit on desktop; the session item shows a note field beside Done
Type a note and click Done
The step resolves with output {resumed_by: "user", note} carrying that text

description: Marking a meta.session Done from the tracked focus rail (tracked/focus-rail.js) offers a note field, and the typed note is sent with Done, on desktop and mobile.
steps: Run a tracked job to a meta.session step
Open its focus rail; a note field sits beside Done
Type a note and click Done
The step resolves with output {resumed_by: "user", note} carrying that text
Repeat on mobile: the same field is there and Done sends the note

description: The answers in a clarifications session's report reach the re-run: the second run sees them in previousSteps and uses them instead of re-asking.
steps: Run a project job whose project.shape returns clarifications[]
In the following 'Answer clarifications' meta.session, answer every question and ask Claude to report back
The session step resolves with output {resumed_by: "report", …} whose answers holds what was typed
Open the second project.shape step's envelope: previousSteps carries that output, with the answers in its top-level answers field
Its brief.md reflects each answer, has no marker for an answered question, and its clarifications[] does not repeat them

description: A project plan asks for content sign-off before the project folder lands: a sign-off meta.session sits after the shaping chain and before the PR that commits it, and a correction re-runs the chain instead of committing.
steps: Run a project job through project.decompose
The next step is a 'Sign off docs/projects/<slug>/' meta.session, before any code.orchestrate-pr step that commits the folder
Its prompt lists brief.md, features.json and roadmap.md to read, taken from the project.* step outputs
Report corrections from the session: the step-review re-runs the affected project.* steps with them and plans another sign-off, and nothing is committed
Report approval from the second sign-off: the landing code.orchestrate-pr runs next

description: project.shape asks at most 5 clarifications, all about scope or appetite; anything else it can't answer is recorded in the brief as an assumption.
steps: Create a project job from a one-sentence idea with nearly every detail missing
Open the project.shape output: clarifications[] has 5 entries or fewer
Each question is about scope, audience or appetite, not an implementation detail
brief.md lists the remaining unknowns as assumptions

description: project.requirements can return clarifications[], and the planner handles them like shape's: an 'Answer clarifications' meta.session, then a second project.requirements that uses the answers.
steps: Run a project job whose brief leaves a behaviour ambiguous
The project.requirements output has a matching clarifications[] entry, and the feature's description carries the [NEEDS CLARIFICATION] marker
The plan has an 'Answer clarifications' meta.session after it, whose prompt lists the questions verbatim, and a second project.requirements
Answer in the session and report back: the second run's features.json resolves the marker and keeps every ID

description: project.decompose can return clarifications[], and the planner handles them like shape's: an 'Answer clarifications' meta.session, then a second project.decompose that uses the answers.
steps: Run a project job where the milestone order depends on an open question (e.g. which of two risky unknowns matters more)
The project.decompose output has a clarifications[] entry for it
The plan has an 'Answer clarifications' meta.session after it, whose prompt lists the questions verbatim, and a second project.decompose
Answer in the session and report back: the second roadmap.md orders the milestones accordingly

description: A project plan ends with a meta.session check after the last milestone, whose prompt walks the user through verifying the project's success criteria.
steps: Open a project job's plan after the step that lands the project folder merges
The step after the last milestone's meta.job is a meta.session
Its prompt lists the brief's success criteria and tells the session to read features.json and walk the quality and still-failing entries
When the step starts, an interactive session opens with that prompt; the step resolves when the user marks it Done or the session reports back (submit_session_report)

description: For a project with any UI, project.requirements writes checkable quality-category entries (look, feel, not generic) whose steps a person or browser driver can follow.
steps: Run project.requirements on a brief for a project with a UI
features.json has entries with category 'quality' covering look, feel and not-generic
Each such entry's steps name a concrete check (a width, a theme, a state, a banned pattern, a threshold), never just 'looks good'

description: An action can screenshot a locally served page through a new narrow, anchored grant that landed as its own approved PR with docs/design/permissions.md updated; a non-local URL is denied.
steps: Find the PR that added the screenshot grant: it touches the permission config or a pinned script plus docs/design/permissions.md, and nothing unrelated
Run an action that screenshots the PWA on localhost: the PNG appears in its output
Make the same action target an external URL: the permission gate denies the call

description: A deterministic UI check (npm run ui:check or equivalent) reports accessibility violations, overflow/clipping, off-token values, generic-AI patterns and console errors, and exits non-zero on any of them.
steps: Run the check on main: it reports each category and exits 0, or lists the known violations
Add a hard-coded colour, an overflowing label, an unlabeled button and a console.error to one PWA screen
Run it again: each seeded problem is reported with its file or selector, and it exits non-zero

description: code.implement-ui writes a token/layout plan with an ASCII wireframe, checks it against banned defaults, builds only from tokens and existing components, and attaches screenshots of its own work to its report.
steps: Run a UI step through code.implement-ui
Its report contains the layout plan with an ASCII wireframe and the banned-defaults check result
Its report includes screenshots of the built screen
The UI check on its diff reports no off-token values

description: code.review-visual reviews with fresh context over a fixed screenshot matrix (widths x light/dark x empty, loading, error, long text), scores a rubric citing screenshots, lists at most 5 located fixes, and says ship or don't ship, and does say don't ship on a bad screen.
steps: Run code.review-visual on a change to one PWA screen
The output contains the full matrix of screenshots
Every rubric score cites at least one of those screenshots
There are 5 fixes or fewer, each naming a file or element
Run it on a deliberately broken screen (clipped text, mixed fonts): the verdict is don't ship

description: code.orchestrate-pr runs the visual review only when the planner sets inputs.lenses to include 'visual'; a UI diff without it gets only code.review-diff.
steps: Run a UI-touching PR step with inputs.lenses: ['visual']: the controller's rounds include code.review-visual
Run a UI-touching PR step without lenses: its rounds include code.review-diff and no visual review

description: The visual loop ends when the reviewer says ship or when two consecutive passes fail to beat the best recorded score, and then keeps the best round, not the last.
steps: Run a visual-lens PR step and open its artifacts: a score is recorded per pass, with the best marked
In a run where two passes in a row score below the best, the loop stops there
The branch's final state matches the best-scoring round's screenshots

description: When reviewer and implementer disagree on taste, the step goes to the user with side-by-side screenshots of the options.
steps: Run a visual-lens PR step until a taste disagreement occurs
The step parks for the user, showing the competing versions side by side
Picking one continues the loop with that version

description: The PWA shows screenshots at a gate on desktop and mobile, viewable full size.
steps: Park a step whose artifacts include screenshots
On desktop, open the gate: the screenshots render inline and open full size on click
On a phone, open the same gate: the screenshots render and can be viewed full size

description: A calibration hold collects the user's good and bad example Outpost screens, and code.review-visual uses them as reference.
steps: At the calibration hold, name a few screens as good and a few as bad
Run code.review-visual afterwards: its output cites the calibration examples in its comparison

description: One existing Outpost screen the user names, rebuilt through the UI loop, is judged better than before by the user.
steps: The user names a screen at the M2 hold
It is rebuilt through a visual-lens PR step
The user compares before and after screenshots at each matrix cell, then uses the screen on desktop and phone
The user says it is better

description: design.language writes a short DESIGN.md of checkable rules and banned defaults plus W3C-format tokens (OKLCH colour, type and spacing scales, light and dark), and renders one style tile the user signs off at a gate.
steps: Run design.language on a project
DESIGN.md is within ~150 lines; each rule can be checked (a value, a ratio, a ban), never just 'be clean'
The tokens file parses as W3C design tokens, colours are OKLCH, and both light and dark sets exist
The job parks at a gate showing the rendered style tile; the folder files land only after sign-off

description: design.language in art-bible mode, for a game, produces an art bible (palette, shape language, sprite scale, animation and HUD rules) with a rendered tile the user signs off.
steps: Run design.language on a game project
The output covers palette, shape language, sprite/tile scale, animation and HUD rules
The gate shows a rendered tile of sample sprites and HUD; the user signs it off

description: design.ux-flows writes user goals, task flows, navigation, ASCII wireframes, a per-component state list and acceptance criteria phrased as observable UI facts.
steps: Run design.ux-flows on a project
Its output has each of those sections, with an ASCII wireframe per main screen
Each component lists its empty, loading, error and populated states
Each acceptance criterion names something a person can see on screen

description: design.gameplay writes a one-page game design: core loop, mechanics, progression/tuning tables and the vertical-slice definition.
steps: Run design.gameplay on a game project
The design fits on one page and states the core loop in one or two sentences
Tuning tables give concrete numbers
The vertical slice is defined as what a player can do in it

description: code.review-ux reviews the running app with heuristics, task walkthroughs and WCAG 2.2 AA, citing evidence for each finding.
steps: Run code.review-ux against a locally served app
Its output walks through each task flow step by step
WCAG 2.2 AA findings name the criterion and the element
On an app with a seeded contrast failure and a keyboard trap, both are reported

description: arch.design writes architecture.md (C4 context and container), a stack choice with the alternatives weighed, ADRs for the binding decisions, and fitness functions wired into CI.
steps: Run arch.design on a project
architecture.md has C4 context and container views within ~150 lines
The stack choice lists at least two alternatives and why each lost
decisions/ has numbered ADRs starting at 0001
The PR adds CI checks for the fitness functions, and violating one makes CI fail

description: Accepted ADRs are binding: a step whose work conflicts with one stops and proposes a superseding ADR instead of overriding it.
steps: Give a child job a task that contradicts an accepted ADR
The step stops and the user sees a proposal for a new ADR that supersedes the old one
The old ADR changes only by a 'Superseded by NNNN' line

description: arch.spike builds a time-boxed throwaway prototype answering one risky question, and reports the answer with evidence without merging the prototype.
steps: Run arch.spike with one question and a time box
Its output answers the question with evidence (a measurement, a screenshot, a log)
The prototype code is not merged into the main branch

description: arch.review runs a fresh-context pre-mortem and scenario review of the brief, design and architecture, and flags scope creep against the brief.
steps: Run arch.review on a project whose architecture includes something the brief lists as a no-go
The output includes a pre-mortem (ways the project fails) and scenario walkthroughs
The no-go item is flagged as scope creep

description: project.check-readiness returns PASS, CONCERNS or FAIL on whether the plan is buildable, with reasons; FAIL stops the job before building.
steps: Run project.check-readiness on a complete project folder: PASS or CONCERNS, with reasons
Remove architecture.md and run it again: FAIL, naming the gap
On FAIL, no build milestone starts

description: project.accept-milestone evaluates a milestone's features end to end with fresh context and is the only thing that sets passes:true, citing evidence in its PR; a feature with only unit-test evidence stays false.
steps: Finish a milestone and run project.accept-milestone
For each feature it passes, its PR cites end-to-end evidence (screenshots, logs or a recorded run of the feature's steps)
A feature whose steps fail in the running app stays passes:false and is reported
A feature backed only by unit tests stays passes:false
git log on features.json shows no other action setting passes:true

description: project.correct-course re-plans a project mid-flight when a milestone shows the roadmap is wrong, keeping finished milestones and reshaping the rest.
steps: Run a project where a finished milestone invalidates a later one
Trigger correct-course: the updated roadmap keeps the finished milestones verbatim and changes the affected later ones
The change and its reason are recorded in progress.md or an ADR

description: project.retro writes a retrospective on a finished project or milestone, naming which actions fell short with evidence.
steps: Run project.retro after a milestone
Its output names specific actions and runs that fell short, citing steps or PRs
Each finding proposes a concrete fix to an action

description: A game can be played by script and captured as frames or a GIF, so reviewers and the user see motion, not stills.
steps: Run scripted play against a locally served browser game
The output includes a GIF or frame sequence of the play
The capture shows the player moving and the game state changing

description: Game review checks HUD legibility over busy scenes, feedback/juice, readability of the core loop in the first 30 seconds, and frame rate, each with evidence from captures.
steps: Run the game review on a game build
Its output scores each of the four criteria and cites a capture for each
Frame rate is reported as a measured number
A build with an unreadable HUD gets a failing HUD score

description: A playtest hold parks the job with a runnable build served over the tailnet and the captures attached; the user opens the build straight from the Outpost app on their phone.
steps: Reach a playtest hold in a game job
The hold shows the captures and a link to the build
Tap the link from the Outpost app on a phone on the tailnet: the game loads and plays
Resume with notes; the next step sees them

description: read.research does web research on a question and returns findings with cited sources that other actions can reuse.
steps: Run read.research with a question (e.g. free licence-clear sound effect packs for a retro arcade game)
Every claim in its output links a source
Opening the links confirms the claims

description: design.source-assets proposes, per asset type, how to produce a game's art and sound (procedural, asset packs, AI generation or tooling) with licence, cost, quality and needed grants; the user approves it at a hold, and any host or key it needs lands as an anchored-grant PR plus a ~/.outpost/.env entry.
steps: Run design.source-assets on a game with an art bible and gameplay doc
The proposal has a recommendation per asset type with licence, cost, quality and grants needed, citing read.research sources
The job parks at a hold showing the proposal
For a recommendation needing a download host or API key, a separate PR adds an anchored grant and the hold names the ~/.outpost/.env entry to set; nothing downloads before both

description: The user tells Outpost to make a game from a short idea, and the job runs end to end with only the holds: no help beyond resuming, answering and approving drafts.
steps: At the M6 hold, the user gives a short game idea
A job is created from it and planned in the project category
It runs through shaping, design, architecture, milestones and acceptance
The user's only input is at holds, check sessions and write-draft approvals; the user never edits the game's code

description: When the user doesn't judge the game good, a retro runs, the actions that fell short are fixed, and the game job is rerun.
steps: After an M6 run the user judges it not good
project.retro runs and names the actions that fell short
PRs fix those actions
A fresh make-a-game job runs with the fixed actions

description: The user judges the game good.
steps: The user plays the finished game from the Outpost app link
The user says it is good

description: Every new permission grant in this project landed as its own PR the user approved, as an anchored whitelist pinned to its destination, with writes only in push.
steps: List the PRs that changed config/permission-groups*.json or any allowlist.json during the project
Each was approved by the user
Each new network or write rule is anchored and pinned to its destination; no rule tries to forbid a flag
The daemon loads every action without assertNotWriteShaped refusing one

description: The repo typechecks and its tests pass at the end of every milestone.
steps: Check out main after the milestone's last PR
npx tsc --noEmit exits 0
npm test exits 0

description: Look: the rebuilt Outpost screen is built only from design tokens and existing .o-* components, and holds up at every screenshot-matrix cell with no overflow or clipping.
steps: Run the UI check on the rebuilt screen: no off-token values, no overflow or clipping
Screenshot it at 375, 768 and 1440 px wide, in light and dark: text never clips or overlaps, and spacing follows the scale
Fill it with long text (60-character names, 500-character bodies): it wraps or truncates with a way to see the rest, and the layout holds
Show it empty, loading and in error: each state has copy and a next action, not a blank area

description: Feel: every interactive element on the rebuilt Outpost screen gives visible hover, focus and pressed feedback, works from the keyboard, and responds without perceptible lag.
steps: Tab through the screen: every control gets a visible focus ring, in a sensible order, with no trap
Hover and press each control: each shows a distinct state
Do the screen's main task by keyboard only
Trigger each action: visible feedback appears within ~100 ms and transitions finish within ~250 ms

description: Not generic: the rebuilt Outpost screen trips none of the generic-AI patterns and reads as part of Outpost rather than a template.
steps: Run the generic-AI-pattern lint: zero hits
Check by eye against the banned list: no purple/blue gradient hero, no stack of identical rounded cards, no emoji as icons, no gratuitous shadows or glassmorphism, no flat type with no hierarchy
Put it beside two screens the user marked good at calibration: it uses the same type scale, spacing and colour roles
Show it to the user without context: they don't say it looks like a template

description: Look: the game matches its signed-off art bible in every captured scene, and its HUD stays legible over its busiest scene.
steps: Put captures of the title screen, gameplay and game-over beside the signed-off tile: palette, shape language and sprite scale match
Capture the busiest gameplay moment: every HUD value is readable at phone width, with text contrast at least 4.5:1 against what's behind it
No placeholder art (default squares, missing-texture colours, stock tutorial sprites) appears anywhere

description: Feel: the game responds instantly and gives feedback for every player action, at a steady frame rate.
steps: Press each control during play: the player responds on the next frame, with no perceptible input lag
Score, hit, pickup and death each have visible feedback (motion, flash, particles or shake) and a sound
Measure frame rate in the busiest scene in a desktop browser: it stays at or above 55 fps
Play on a phone over the tailnet: touch controls work and the game stays playable

description: Readable and not generic: a new player grasps the game's goal within 30 seconds without instructions, and the game has something distinctive rather than reading as a tutorial clone.
steps: Give the game to someone who hasn't seen it, with no explanation: within 30 seconds they can say what they're trying to do
Show the user the captures without context: they name at least one thing distinctive to this game (a mechanic, art choice or feel)
The user doesn't say it looks like a template or tutorial project

description: A settled meta.session always triggers a step-review, whether it settles by submit_session_report or by Done, and a report with corrections, answers or wantsReplan makes the planner re-plan.
steps: Run a job to a meta.session step and click Done with no note
The job's events show a step-review run for that step, which ends in submit_continue with the plan unchanged
Run another meta.session and have Claude report back with wantsReplan: true and a correction
On a job with manual plan review, a step-review runs, sees the report in the step's output, and the job goes to plan review with an amended plan

description: An action step's submit_replan_request reaches the planner at once with its reason, and the job is left unfailed.
steps: Run a job whose action step finds a false premise in its inputs and calls submit_replan_request with a reason
The step shows 'Asked for a replan: <reason>' and is in replan_requested, neither failed nor resolved
meta.orchestrate starts in replan mode without waiting for the step's parallel group, and its envelope's replanRequest carries the step id, action, reason, evidence and suggestion
On a job with manual plan review, the amended plan waits for the user's plan approval; the job never shows as failed
A second replan request from the same step after that amendment fails the step with 'asked for a replan twice'
In a meta.session, have Claude call submit_replan_request at the user's direction: the step goes to replan_requested and the planner starts in replan mode the same way

description: A controller's replan move does the same as an action step's request: the planner runs at once with its reason and the job is left unfailed.
steps: Run a code.orchestrate-pr step whose controller submits next: {kind: "replan", reason}
The step goes to replan_requested and its session closes; the job does not fail
meta.orchestrate starts in replan mode with the controller's reason in replanRequest
While a dispatch of that controller is still running, the same move is refused by validateNext
A dispatched child of the controller that calls submit_replan_request is refused, whether it passes its dispatchId or its dispatch id as stepId, and the controller's step stays as it was

description: meta.wait is gone from the catalog and the install dir, and a plan-level delaySec soak holds the step it's set on.
steps: With an unedited installed copy, restart the daemon: ~/.outpost/actions/meta/wait is deleted and meta.wait is not in the planner's action catalog
With an edited ~/.outpost/actions/meta/wait/SKILL.md, restart the daemon: the dir moves to ~/.outpost/actions/.retired/meta/wait/, an event is logged, and meta.wait is not in the catalog
Approve a plan with delaySec: 120 on its second step
After the first step settles, the second shows 'Starts in 2m · Start now' on desktop and mobile and doesn't start early
It starts on its own once the delay elapses; on another run, Start now starts it at once
Restart the daemon mid-delay: the step still shows the remaining 'Starts in …' and starts on time
